IMPASTO: Integrating Model-Based Planning with
Learned Dynamics Models for Robotic Oil Painting Reproduction
Yingke Wang1, Hao Li1, Yifeng Zhu2, Hong-Xing Yu1,
Ken Goldberg3, Li Fei-Fei1, Jiajun Wu1, Yunzhu Li4, and Ruohan Zhang1
Fig. 1: IMPASTO is a robotic oil painting system that integrates learned neural dynamics models with model-based planning
algorithms to replicate human artists’ brushstrokes and artworks.
Abstract— Robotic reproduction of oil paintings using soft
brushes and pigments requires force-sensitive control of de-
formable tools, prediction of brushstroke effects, and multi-step
stroke planning, often without human step-by-step demonstra-
tions or faithful simulators. Given only a sequence of target
oil painting images, can a robot infer and execute the stroke
trajectories, forces, and colors needed to reproduce it? We
present IMPASTO, a robotic oil-painting system that integrates
learned pixel dynamics models with model-based planning. The
dynamics models predict canvas updates from image obser-
vations and parameterized stroke actions; a receding-horizon
model predictive control optimizer then plans trajectories and
forces, while a force-sensitive controller executes strokes on a
7-DoF robot arm. IMPASTO integrates low-level force control,
learned dynamics models, and high-level closed-loop planning,
learns solely from robot self-play, and approximates human
artists’ single-stroke datasets and multi-stroke artworks, out-
performing baselines in reproduction accuracy. Project website:
https://impasto-robopainting.github.io/.
I. INTRODUCTION
Robot painting reproduction—enabling machines to ac-
curately replicate physical artworks with brushes and
pigments—has a rich history and presents unique technical
challenges [1, 2]. In modern times, these robots often paint
images on canvas by executing sequences of brushstrokes and
adjusting based on sensory feedback [1, 3, 4]. Unlike digital
image generation, a painting robot must master complex
low-level control of deformable tools and fluids, force-
sensitive manipulation of a brush against a surface, visual
perception of the evolving artwork, and high-level planning
1Stanford University.

4Columbia University.of stroke sequences. These requirements make robot painting
reproduction a significant challenge: the robot must achieve
the same nuanced, variable brushstrokes as a human artist
based on real-world physics.
We ask:Given only a sequence of static images of an oil
painting by an expert artist, can a robot infer corresponding
control actions, such as trajectory, orientation, and applied
force, to approximately reproduce the painting?This setting
is similar to art training exercises—can our robot reach the
level of beginning art students who are able to replicate
an oil painting? This is a challenging setting for robotics,
as it simultaneously 1) requires precise low-level control to
replicate strokes with soft brushes and wet paints; 2) requires
high-level planning to compose multiple strokes; 3) assumes
no access to any form of action demonstration data, either
through teleoperation or tracking the brushes.
One approach to tackling this challenge islearning a
2D dynamics modelfor the oil painting domain. Given the
current visual state of the canvas, and a parameterized action,
the robot should predict the consequence of its brush action,
i.e., the resulting state of the canvas. We conjecture that
such a model can be trained through self-play. Once trained,
the robot can integrate this model with model predictive
control (MPC) applied within local stroke windows to infer
actions to replicate each brushstroke, plan multiple strokes
to approximate a complex painting. Although learning neural
dynamics models and combining them with MPC have
become increasingly popular in different robotic tasks [5–
9], we believe this is the first attempt to leverage them for
robot painting.
We presentIMPASTO(IntegratingModel-Based
Planning with LeArned DynamicSModels for RoboTicarXiv:2603.29315v1  [cs.RO]  31 Mar 2026

Oil Painting Reproduction), a robotic system that combines
learned dynamics models with force-sensitive control and
model-based planning to approximately reproduce human
oil paintings. Our contributions include:
•Learned pixel dynamics model: We develop a neural
network dynamics model of brushstrokes, trained on
a dataset of robot self-play data. This model learns
the complex relationship between the robot’s action
parameters (end-effector trajectory, applied force) and
the resulting stroke outcomes to predict stroke shape
and appearance.
•Model predictive trajectory and force planning: We
integrate the learned model into a model-based planning
framework for single or consecutive stroke planning.
Given a desired appearance of stroke(s), the MPC
optimizer computes precise trajectories and forces to
reproduce each brushstroke.
•An integrated robot painting system: We implement
a complete system on a 7-DoF robotic arm with a
force-torque sensor. The system autonomously handles
dipping the brush in paint, cleaning the brush between
colors, and painting the strokes on a canvas.
We evaluate IMPASTO on both individual strokes and
full paintings drawn by expert human artists. Our results
suggest that the learned model plus model-based planning
approach yields strokes that closely match the appearances
of the human brushstrokes. We demonstrate that the learned
dynamics model can better replicate individual and overlaid
strokes than the baseline methods. We also show closed-loop
painting experiments in which the robot plans and paints a
multi-stroke artwork.
II. RELATEDWORK
A. Modern Robot Painting
The idea of automating art dates back centuries [1].
Harold Cohen’s AARON in 1986 is widely considered the
first modern robot painter with an open-loop programmed
approach [10]. Recently, painting robots have employed
closed-loop control. e-David is an industrial robotic arm
equipped with a camera that paints with real brushes and
continuously adjusts its strategy based on visual feedback
[3, 11]. Another state-of-the-art system is the FRIDA series
[4, 12, 13], a collaborative painting robot that introduces a
differentiable simulation for brushstrokes and a real2sim2real
planning loop. FRIDA simulates how each stroke will appear
and, during execution, periodically captures an image of the
canvas to re-plan the remaining strokes, though FRIDA’s
primary goal was not exact reproduction of existing artworks.
These modern robotic painting systems emphasize sophis-
ticated stroke planning algorithms, from high-level image
segmentation and stroke sequencing [3] to optimization of
stroke parameters in simulation [4], all aimed at achieving
human-like painting results under robotic control.
Recent advances in robotic painting leverage machine
learning methods. Researchers have applied reinforcement
learning (RL) to optimize paint coverage [14, 15] and strokeplanning [16–18], used genetic algorithms for stroke plan-
ning [19], used imitation learning (IL) to leverage human
demonstrations [20, 21], and employed deep generative mod-
els to synthesize and stylize brushstrokes [22–25]. Together,
these approaches push robotic art beyond hand-designed
programming toward more autonomous and creative behav-
iors. It is worth noticing that our problem setting is among
the most challenging ones: We aim to closely approximate
human experts’ brushstrokes with soft brushes and wet
pigments. Unlike in the RL settings, we do not rely on a
painting simulator; unlike in the IL setting, we do not have
access to human demonstrations.
B. Planning with Learned Neural Dynamics Models
Deep neural networks trained on interaction data have
become a standard way to learn dynamics models for manip-
ulation, with broad empirical success [6, 7]. Such models can
be trained directly in pixel space [26–30] or in compact latent
spaces that abstract observations [8, 31–35]. Beyond these
representations, structured scene encodings improve model-
ing fidelity and generalization, including keypoints [36–39],
particles [40–42], and mesh-based parameterizations [9]. For
robot painting, a pixel-based dynamics model is a natural
choice. Planning over learned dynamics is difficult due to
their nonlinearity and nonconvexity. A prevalent strategy is
online sampling-based optimization, most commonly cross-
entropy methods (CEM) [43] and Model Predictive Path
Integral (MPPI) [44], as used by prior work for planning
in manipulation tasks [5, 27, 29, 37, 45–47]. These methods
require a large number of samples as the action dimension
grows. Meanwhile, gradient-based trajectory optimization
[40, 48] is prone to local minima and non-smooth objectives.
III. METHOD
We describe the parameterization of brushstrokes, color
prediction, the hardware system setup for oil painting, the
architecture design and training of the dynamics model,
the multi-step planning algorithm, and baseline methods for
comparison.

We separate color estimation from shape prediction, so

IV. EXPERIMENTS ANDRESULTS
Our experiments are designed to address three key ques-
tions:Q1. How much data is needed to train a dynamics
model in our case?Q2. Can IMPASTO reproduce expert
human artists’ strokes with low error and high visual sim-
ilarity?Q3. Can IMPASTO enable closed-loop, multi-step
planning to approximate a given oil painting?
Fig. 5: Training and evaluationL ℓ1(unweighted) of
IMPASTO’s dynamics model vs. number of training samples

Q1. Can IMPASTO’s pixel dynamics model be trained to
predict the stroke effects with high fidelity?
As shown in Fig. 5, as the number of training samples
increases, the dynamics model achieves lower prediction
error when predicting the next canvas state. The validation set
is fixed at 10% of the total dataset size. We observe that with
a reasonable amount of self-play data (n= 900), the model
can achieve a prediction with unweightedL ℓ1= 0.0285.
Q2. Can IMPASTO reproduce human individual strokes
with lower error and higher visual similarity than baseline
methods?
We compare IMPASTO-UNet with the baselines. Since
real brush-paint interaction is inherently stochastic, we ex-
plicitly controlled the execution conditions in the final re-
ported experiments. In particular, we matched the brush state
and pigment condition for each stroke across baselines as
close as possible, in order to reduce variability across trials
and improve fairness in quantitative comparisons.
First, we collected two datasets for evaluation. The first
dataset (“Single Strokes”) comes from five trained human
artists, who are experts in oil painting. Every artist con-
tributed 12 separate brushstrokes that reflected their unique
style. The second dataset (“Overlaid Strokes”) was produced
by the robot, which freely painted 50 random strokes that
were layered on top of each other. Note that these datasets
are not used for training.
Then we integrate the learned dynamics model with the
multi-step planning algorithm described in Sec. III-E. We
first set the planning horizon to be 1 step. We measure the
accuracy in two stages: the planning stage and the execution
stage. At the planning stage, the 1-step planning algorithm in-
fers the stroke actions, then we use IMPASTO and baselines
to predict and render the strokes, and compare the rendered
strokes with ground-truth strokes. At the execution stage, we
let the robot execute the stroke action, take a photo of the
canvas, and compare that with the ground truth.

prediction window. We compare IMPASTO with FRIDA-
CNN, the best performing baseline other than IMPASTO’s

V. CONCLUSIONS
An oil painting robot must address fine-grained control
of deformable tools and fluid dynamics, execute force-
sensitive brush-surface interactions, perceive the evolving
canvas state, and solve high-level planning of stroke se-
quences. These requirements make robotic oil painting an
inspiring and ambitious challenge for robotics research. We
present IMPASTO, a robot painting system that integrates
learned dynamics models and model-based planning to ap-
proximate oil paintings. We demonstrate that IMPASTO
can approximate human artists’ brushstrokes and artworks.
Through these contributions, we advance robotic painting by
fusing learning and control: the robot gains an understanding
of brush dynamics from data and uses it in a principled
planning framework. IMPASTO represents a step toward
robots that can paint with the finesse of a human artist,
manipulating real brushes and paints.

We use a 7-DoF Franka Emika Panda equipped with a

a grounding wire to the data-acquisition module’s adapter.
Sensor readouts are first bias-corrected (offset removal) at
the beginning of each primitive skill and then smoothed with

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary: The partial document describes IMPASTO, a robotic oil painting system that integrates learned neural dynamics models with model-based planning to reproduce human artworks. The system aims to infer and execute stroke trajectories, forces, and colors from a sequence of target oil painting images, without relying on human demonstrations or faithful simulators. Key contributions include a learned pixel dynamics model trained through robot self-play, model predictive control for planning trajectories and forces, and an integrated robotic system with force-sensitive control. The document also discusses related work in modern robot painting and planning with learned neural dynamics models, highlighting IMPASTO's unique approach of learning solely from self-play and approximating human artists' work without demonstrations. The methodology section outlines the brushstroke model, color prediction, hardware setup, dynamics model architecture and training, and planning algorithms.

structure.title: RELATEDWORK
structure.summary:
This partial document describes IMPASTO, a robotic system designed to reproduce human oil paintings. The main points covered are:

*   **Learned Pixel Dynamics Model:** A neural network is developed to learn the complex relationship between robot actions (trajectory, force) and the resulting brushstroke appearance, trained on robot self-play data.
*   **Model Predictive Control for Planning:** The learned dynamics model is integrated into a planning framework (Model Predictive Control - MPC) to compute optimal trajectories and forces for creating individual or consecutive brushstrokes.
*   **Integrated Robotic Painting System:** A complete system is implemented on a 7-DoF robotic arm with force-sensing capabilities, capable of autonomously handling tasks like dipping the brush in paint, cleaning it, and painting on a canvas.
*   **Evaluation:** The system is evaluated on individual strokes and full paintings, demonstrating that the learned model and planning approach closely match human brushstrokes and outperform baseline methods.
*   **Related Work:** The document reviews existing modern robot painting systems, highlighting their approaches to automation, control (open-loop vs. closed-loop), and the use of machine learning techniques like reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and generative models. It also discusses planning with learned neural dynamics models, including different modeling approaches and optimization strategies.
*   **Methodology (Brushstroke Model):** The document begins to detail the methodology, specifically focusing on the parameterization of brushstrokes, which are represented by quadratic Bézier curves with parameters for location, length, bend, orientation, force (affecting thickness), and color.

structure.title: METHOD
structure.summary:
This partial document describes IMPASTO, a robotic system designed to reproduce human oil paintings. The main points covered are:

*   **Learned Pixel Dynamics Model:** A neural network is developed to model the complex relationship between robot actions (trajectory, force) and the resulting brushstroke appearance. This model is trained on robot self-play data.
*   **Model Predictive Control for Planning:** The learned dynamics model is integrated into a model-based planning framework (Model Predictive Control - MPC) to determine optimal trajectories and forces for individual or consecutive brushstrokes, aiming to achieve a desired appearance.
*   **Integrated Robotic Painting System:** A complete system is implemented using a 7-DoF robotic arm with a force-torque sensor. This system autonomously handles tasks like dipping the brush in paint, cleaning it, and executing strokes on a canvas.
*   **Evaluation and Comparison:** The system is evaluated on individual strokes and full paintings. Results indicate that the learned model and planning approach produce strokes closely matching human brushstrokes and outperform baseline methods.
*   **Related Work:** The document reviews existing modern robot painting systems, highlighting their approaches to automation, control, and planning, and discusses the challenges of replicating expert human brushstrokes with soft brushes and wet pigments. It also covers advancements in planning with learned neural dynamics models.
*   **Methodology Details:** Specifics are provided on:
    *   **Brushstroke Model:** Parameterization of brushstrokes using a quadratic Bezier curve with parameters like starting location, length, bend, orientation, force, and color.
    *   **Color Prediction:** A separate module for estimating color based on pigment databases.
    *   **Hardware System:** The use of a Franka Emika Panda robot arm, a force-torque sensor, a brush, a palette, a brush cleaner, and a camera for visual feedback.
    *   **Robot Control:** Implementation of force control along the surface normal and impedance control for stroke execution.
    *   **Pixel Dynamics Model Architecture:** Details on the U-Net based encoder-decoder architecture for predicting the next image observation given the current observation and a stroke action.

nodes.title: Brushstroke Model
nodes.summary:
The document describes IMPASTO, a system for robotic oil painting. It covers the following main points:

*   **Brushstroke Parameterization:** A brushstroke is represented by six parameters: starting location, stroke length, bend, in-plane orientation, normal force (affecting paint thickness and width), and color. This representation is compared to previous work (FRIDA), highlighting the use of a force parameter for sensitive control.
*   **Color Prediction:** A separate module is used to predict the paint color (RGB+Alpha) by performing a nearest-neighbor search on a pigment database.
*   **Hardware System and Robot Control:** The system uses a Franka Emika Panda robot arm equipped with a force/torque sensor for precise force control. It details the robot's control in impedance mode and the implementation of a force loop for normal force accumulation. The hardware setup includes a specific brush, palette trays, a brush cleaner, and a top-down camera for observation.
*   **Pixel Dynamics Model:** A core component is a differentiable forward dynamics model that predicts the next canvas observation given the current image and a stroke action. The model uses a U-Net architecture with an image encoder and an action encoder. It also describes how stroke actions are pre-rendered into images to bridge the modality gap.
*   **Dataset and Training:** The robot self-supervises to collect data for training the dynamics model. The training objective is a weighted L1 loss that emphasizes changes near the stroke. Data augmentation techniques are also mentioned.
*   **Multi-Step Stroke Planning:** The learned dynamics model enables multi-step planning using Model Predictive Control (MPC) in a receding-horizon fashion. The system optimizes a sequence of actions to reach a target image, executing a subset of actions before replanning.
*   **Baseline Methods:** Several baseline methods are introduced for comparison, including IMPASTO-LR (a linear regressor approach), Heuristics-only (single-step planning), and FRIDA-CNN (using FRIDA's param2stroke model). A key distinction is made that IMPASTO predicts the full next state image, while baselines often predict only the incremental stroke.
*   **Experiments and Results:** The document outlines experiments to evaluate the dynamics model's fidelity, IMPASTO's ability to reproduce human strokes, and its performance in multi-step planning. It presents results showing how prediction error decreases with more training data and compares IMPASTO's performance against baselines using metrics like weighted L1 loss and LPIPS.

structure.title: EXPERIMENTS ANDRESULTS
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt details a system called IMPASTO for robotic oil painting. It focuses on integrating learned dynamics models with model-based planning to achieve realistic brushstroke reproduction and complex artwork approximation.

The main points covered are:

*   **Receding-Horizon MPC with Adaptive Covariance (Algorithm 1):** This outlines the core planning algorithm, which uses Model Predictive Control (MPC) to iteratively plan actions over a receding horizon. It incorporates adaptive covariance for sampling candidate actions and uses an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) for refining the action sequence.
*   **Baselines and Comparison Methods:** The document describes and compares IMPASTO with other methods:
    *   **Heuristics-only:** A simpler approach for single-step stroke planning based on skeletonization.
    *   **FRIDA-CNN:** A variant of the FRIDA system that uses a CNN to predict stroke occupancy fields.
    *   **IMPASTO-LR:** A linear regression variant of IMPASTO.
    *   **IMPASTO-UNet:** The main U-Net-based IMPASTO model.
*   **Experimental Setup and Evaluation:**
    *   **Data Requirements:** Investigates how much data is needed to train the dynamics model.
    *   **Stroke Reproduction:** Evaluates IMPASTO's ability to reproduce individual human artist strokes in terms of error (weighted L1 loss) and visual similarity (LPIPS). Datasets include "Single Strokes" from human artists and "Overlaid Strokes" generated by the robot.
    *   **Multi-step Planning:** Assesses IMPASTO's capability to approximate complex oil paintings using closed-loop, multi-step planning with a defined horizon.
*   **Key Findings and Results:**
    *   The dynamics model's prediction error decreases with more training data.
    *   IMPASTO-UNet generally outperforms baselines (FRIDA-CNN, Heuristics-only) in both planning and execution stages, particularly in terms of LPIPS (perceptual similarity).
    *   IMPASTO demonstrates good generalization to human stroke styles even when trained on self-play data.
    *   IMPASTO is effective in handling noisy base images (overlaid strokes).
    *   For multi-step planning, IMPASTO shows significant improvements over FRIDA-CNN in both planning and execution metrics.
    *   Qualitative results (figures) showcase IMPASTO's ability to reproduce individual strokes and approximate complex paintings with high visual fidelity.
*   **Conclusion:** IMPASTO represents a significant advancement in robotic painting by fusing learned dynamics models with principled planning, enabling robots to paint with human-like finesse.

nodes.title: PLANNING
nodes.summary:
The provided document excerpt details several components of a system, likely for image manipulation or generation. Key points include:

*   **Pixel Dynamics Model:** A neural network architecture (Fig. A2) is used to model pixel dynamics. This model classifies pixels based on a color patch database (Fig. A3) using a Mahalanobis metric and estimates covariances. Transparency is determined by a ratio comparing observed color change to palette-to-base contrast.
*   **Planning Module (Appendix C):**
    *   **PCA-RANSAC Multi-way Splitter:** This component segments difference maps between base and target images into disjoint stroke masks. It uses k-means for initial segmentation, local PCA for feature extraction, and RANSAC to robustly fit lines or quadratic curves to define candidate stroke masks. These masks are then selected to maximize coverage while penalizing curvature and overlap, and finally thickened into single-connected strokes. This process yields initializations for MPPI optimization. Visualizations of the splitter's output are shown in Fig. A4.
    *   **Stochastic Sampling with CMA-Style Adaptive Covariance:** This describes the sampling process within an MPPI optimization iteration. A candidate set of control sequences is generated by perturbing a nominal sequence with time-indexed Gaussian noise, scaled by a Cholesky factor of the covariance structure. The elite candidates are selected based on terminal cost, and their weights are used to update the nominal sequence via an exponential moving average. Covariance adaptation is performed in a CMA-style manner, updating step-size and covariance paths.
*   **Additional Results (Appendix D):** The document mentions that for complex paintings shown in a video, a robot follows a human artist using CMA-ES. Additional visualization results comparing human and robot strokes are presented in Figs. A5, A6, and A7.
